section.title: Let the Peoples Praise You
section.sectionRationale: A brief harvest prayer built on the Aaronic blessing, this psalm asks God to bless Israel not as an end in itself but so that His way and salvation would be known among all nations, joining a specific, tangible harvest to the missionary hope that every people on earth would come to praise the true God.
section.thesis: God's blessing on His own people is never meant to stop with them, for His grace toward Israel exists so that His way may be known on earth and His salvation among all nations, a missionary purpose fulfilled in the gospel going out to every people through Christ, in whom the whole earth is called to praise God and fear Him.
section.frameNote: Three movements: a prayer, echoing the Aaronic blessing, that God's grace on His people would make His way known among the nations, verses 1-2; a refrain calling all peoples to praise God as He judges justly and guides the nations, verses 3-5; and the closing report that the earth has yielded its harvest, with the hope that all the earth will fear Him, verses 6-7.

units.label: That Your ways may be known on earth
units.note: the Aaronic blessing prayed for a missionary purpose

verses.text: May God be gracious to us and bless us, and cause His face to {{panim|shine}} upon us, Selah
that Your ways may be known on earth, Your salvation among all nations.

units.label: Let the peoples praise You, O God
units.note: the refrain calling all nations to praise the just Judge

verses.text: Let the peoples praise You, O God; let all the peoples praise You.
Let the nations be glad and sing for joy, for You judge the peoples justly and lead the nations of the earth. Selah
Let the peoples praise You, O God; let all the peoples praise You.

units.label: The earth has yielded its harvest
units.note: the closing hope that all the earth will fear God

verses.text: The earth has yielded its harvest; God, our God, blesses us.
God blesses us, that all the ends of the earth shall {{yare|fear}} Him.

panim.gloss: Face, presence. To have God's face shine is to enjoy His favorable, personal presence, the language of the Aaronic blessing, Numbers 6:24-26, here repurposed not as a private comfort but as the very means by which the nations will come to know God's way.

yare.gloss: To fear, to stand in reverent awe. The psalm's closing hope is that this reverence for God would extend to 'all the ends of the earth,' turning God's specific blessing on Israel into a global, missionary purpose.

basic.context: This short psalm echoes the priestly blessing of Numbers 6, but turns it outward, asking God to bless His people specifically so that His way and salvation would become known to every nation. It closes by connecting a good, tangible harvest to this same missionary hope.
basic.hermeneutics: The psalm teaches that God's blessings on His covenant people were never meant to terminate on them alone; they exist so that the whole earth would come to know and praise the true God.
basic.originalLanguages: The prayer that God's panim, face, would shine on His people borrows the language of the Aaronic blessing, Numbers 6:24-26, but redirects it toward the missionary hope that all the earth would yare, fear, reverence, the true God.
basic.typology: This psalm's hope that 'all the ends of the earth' would come to fear God anticipates the Great Commission, where the risen Christ sends His disciples to make disciples of all nations, Matthew 28:19, fulfilling in the gospel what this psalm could only pray for in hope.
basic.christ: Christ is the fulfillment of this psalm's missionary hope, for in Him God's way and salvation have indeed become known among all nations, as the gospel goes out to every people at His own command, Matthew 28:19, and as every tribe, tongue, and nation is gathered to praise Him, Revelation 7:9-10.
basic.god: God is shown as gracious blesser of His own people, just judge and guide of every nation, and provider of the earth's tangible harvest, whose ultimate purpose in all of this blessing is that the whole earth would come to know and reverently fear Him.
basic.crossReferences: Numbers 6:24-26 supplies the priestly blessing this psalm echoes and redirects toward the nations. Matthew 28:19 records Christ's command to make disciples of all nations, the fulfillment of this psalm's missionary hope. Revelation 7:9-10 pictures a great multitude from every nation, tribe, and language praising God, the psalm's prayer answered in full.
basic.oneStory: This psalm's prayer that God's blessing on His people would make His way known among all nations finds its fulfillment in Christ, who sends His people to every nation with the gospel, gathering at last a multitude from every tribe and tongue to praise the God this psalm calls all peoples to worship.

context.literary:
Psalm 67 is seven verses long, and its design is part of its message. The refrain of verses 3 and 5, 'Let the peoples praise You, O God; let all the peoples praise You,' stands like two pillars with verse 4 between them, and the whole psalm can be read as an inward-turning and then outward-turning shape. Verses 1 and 2 ask for blessing on 'us.' Verses 3 to 5 widen to 'the peoples' and 'the nations.' Verses 6 and 7 come home to 'us' again, but now with the goal stated: 'that all the ends of the earth shall fear Him.' The psalm begins with a small circle and ends with the largest one, and the small circle is always on the way to the large.

The word 'earth' carries the same movement. It appears in verse 2 ('known on earth'), verse 4 ('the nations of the earth'), verse 6 ('The earth has yielded its harvest') and verse 7 ('the ends of the earth'). The earth in verse 6 is soil that gives grain, and the earth in verse 7 is the human world that gives praise. The psalm lets the first lead to the second, so that a good harvest becomes a sign that the God of one nation is the God of the whole planet.

The verb 'bless' binds the psalm together as well: it opens verse 1 and closes both verses 6 and 7. The psalm begins with a request, 'may God... bless us,' and ends with a statement, 'God blesses us,' so the prayer of the first line is treated as already being answered by the last. Only the divine name varies. Throughout the psalm the writer says 'God,' Elohim, the name that belongs to all peoples, and not the covenant name, which suits a prayer addressed to the nations' ears. Selah at verses 1 and 4 marks two pauses, the first after the blessing and the second after the statement of God's rule.

The psalm is a song, as the heading indicates, and its brevity and repetition would make it easy to sing in a large gathering. It is the kind of text a congregation could learn in one hearing and carry home.
context.historical:
The psalm has no named author in the BSB text, and its setting can only be inferred. Verse 6 speaks of the harvest as already given, and most readers think of a festival of ingathering, such as the Feast of Weeks or the Feast of Booths, when the people brought the first and the final fruits, Deuteronomy 16:9-17. Those festivals were joyful, communal and public, and they were also the occasions when the nations were most likely to be noticed. Solomon's prayer at the temple asks that foreigners who hear of God's name and pray toward the house be heard 'so that all the peoples of the earth may know Your name and fear You,' 1 Kings 8:41-43, and Psalm 67 sounds very like that prayer in a short form.

The psalm borrows its opening from the priestly blessing that Aaron's sons were told to speak over Israel, Numbers 6:22-27. The priests were to 'put My name' on the people, and the people's blessing was a mark of God's presence among them. Israel's life in the land was lived under that blessing: rain in its season, flocks, fields and peace. Yet the nations around knew these blessings from other sources, and they sacrificed to Baal and the gods of fertility to secure them. The psalm claims that the harvest comes from the one God, 'our God,' and so it is a quiet claim against the gods of the land and of the nations.

The worldview behind the psalm is the promise to Abraham. God had said He would bless Abraham and make him a blessing, and that all the families of the earth would be blessed through him, Genesis 12:2-3. Every prosperous season in Israel was a fresh evidence that the promise was intact, and every lean season was a reason to ask again. The psalm does not ask for blessing in order to win rivalry with the nations. It asks for blessing so that they will turn.
context.canonical:
Psalm 67 is a hinge in the Psalter's witness to the nations. It echoes the priestly blessing of Numbers 6:24-26, takes the promise of Genesis 12:3 and 22:18 as its ground, and opens into the nations' praise in psalms such as 96, 98 and 117. Psalm 117 is only two verses and calls the nations to praise for God's steadfast love, and Psalm 67 gives the prayer that precedes it. The two can be read as a prayer and its answer.

The prophets carry the same vision forward. Isaiah 2:2-4 sees the nations streaming to the mountain of the LORD to learn His ways, and Isaiah 49:6 gives the servant as 'a light for the nations' so that God's salvation may reach 'to the ends of the earth.' Zechariah 8:20-23 pictures people from many cities and peoples taking hold of a Jew's garment and saying 'Let us go with you, for we have heard that God is with you.' Malachi 1:11 says God's name will be great among the nations.

The New Testament sees itself as the answer. Paul quotes the Old Testament on the Gentiles' praise in Romans 15:9-11 and says that the Scripture foresaw that God would justify the Gentiles by faith and announced the gospel to Abraham in advance, Galatians 3:8. Paul and Barnabas turn to the Gentiles in Acts 13:47, citing Isaiah 49:6. James quotes the prophets at the Jerusalem council to show that the Gentiles are being gathered in, Acts 15:13-18. In Revelation 7:9 the multitude stands from 'every nation, tribe, people and tongue,' and Revelation 21:24-26 has the nations bringing their glory into the city. The psalm's last line, 'all the ends of the earth shall fear Him,' meets its goal there.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The psalmist means for Israel to read its own blessings differently. A congregation that prays 'bless us' is in danger of hearing only the first half. Psalm 67 forbids that. Its second verse begins with a purpose clause, 'that Your ways may be known on earth,' and its last verse repeats the purpose, 'that all the ends of the earth shall fear Him.' The blessing is real and is prayed for with open hands, but it is a means. It is given so that the world might look at Israel and see God.

The writer also wants the nations to be treated as persons who can be glad, not merely as subjects or rivals. Verse 4 invites them to 'be glad and sing for joy,' and gives the reason: God 'judge[s] the peoples justly and lead[s] the nations.' A worshiping Israel was meant to picture a world that would rejoice under God's rule, not one that would be crushed by it. The prayer was also a check on pride. To ask for blessing so that others would fear God was to give up any idea that the blessing belonged to Israel alone.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm describes a prayer and a report. It records the words a congregation sang and the harvest they received, and it does not tell anyone to pray for a harvest or to sing it in any particular way. The prescriptive force comes from its shape. A request for blessing that is tied to a purpose for the nations is a model for any later prayer.

There is a danger in misreading the psalm as a promise that every blessing will be material, or that God will always bless the faithful with good harvests. Verse 6 reports a harvest, it does not guarantee one. Elsewhere Scripture recognises lean years even for the faithful, Habakkuk 3:17-18. What carries forward is the direction of the prayer: the church asks to be blessed in order that the nations may come to know the God who blesses, and it receives good gifts as a trust for that end, 2 Corinthians 9:8-11.

debates.question: Is the harvest in verse 6 already past, or is it a prayer for the future?

views.label: A completed harvest, celebrated
views.case: The Hebrew verb in verse 6 is in a form that normally describes completed action, so the psalm would be sung at a thanksgiving after the ingathering. On this reading the earlier requests, in verses 1 to 5, are grounded in the fact that God has already shown His goodness in the fields.

views.label: A certain promise, stated as if done
views.case: Hebrew prophetic and liturgical speech often uses the completed form for what God will surely do, sometimes called the prophetic perfect. The psalm would then be confident petition: God's blessing is so sure that the writer speaks as if it had happened. Verse 7, with its future-sounding 'shall fear,' would fit that tone.

views.label: A sign that leads into petition
views.case: Some see the last two verses as a bridge: the harvest given is the pledge that the larger blessing, the nations' turning, will follow. The past gift and the future hope belong to one movement and need not be separated.

debates.bearing: The tense question does not change the psalm's argument. A gift already received or a gift promised both serve the same purpose, and the congregation is invited to read ordinary blessing as evidence of God's larger plan.

debates.question: Does the psalm look for the nations' conversion or only for their awe?

views.label: A true turning to God
views.case: The psalm asks that God's 'salvation' be known 'among all nations' and that the peoples praise Him, repeatedly. The verb 'fear' in verse 7 in the Old Testament is also the word for the reverence that belongs to covenant worship. Isaiah 45:22-23 and Zechariah 2:11 support a hope in which the nations actually join God's people.

views.label: Recognition of God's rule
views.case: Others point out that the psalm does not mention the nations joining Israel, and that the language of God 'leading' and 'judging' them could describe acknowledgment of His sovereignty without a full covenant relationship. Psalm 66:3, for instance, speaks of enemies who 'cower.'

debates.bearing: The words 'salvation,' 'glad' and 'sing for joy' favour the stronger reading, and the New Testament takes it that way, Acts 13:47-48. Whichever is chosen, the psalm makes the nations the object of prayer, which is itself a large step.

study.originalLanguages:
Start with the opening of the psalm, which borrows three verbs from Numbers 6:25: God be gracious, bless, and cause His face to shine. The word for 'be gracious' is the root behind 'grace' and describes favour given freely, without being earned. The verb 'to shine' is the same one used in Numbers 6:25, and the image is of a face lit up with delight. To see God's face shining is to know that He is pleased. The Aaronic blessing has three lines, each with two petitions, and in the psalm the last clause of the blessing is replaced: where Numbers 6 goes on to 'lift up His countenance toward you and give you peace,' Psalm 67 goes on to 'that Your ways may be known.' The peace of the blessing is turned into the purpose of the blessing.

Two words in verse 2 deserve attention. 'Ways' is the Hebrew derekh, the road or course of life, and in the Psalms it often names the path God walks and the path He asks His people to walk, as in Psalm 25:4 and Psalm 103:7. To pray that His 'way' be known on earth is to pray that the nations would learn how He acts, in mercy and justice. The second word is 'salvation,' yeshuah, which has the same root as the name Yeshua, or Jesus. In the Old Testament it covers deliverance of every kind, from enemies, from sickness, from death. To ask that it be known 'among all nations' is to pray that the rescue God gives Israel would be recognised as available to everyone.

Verse 4 gives the reason the nations can sing: God 'judge[s] the peoples justly and lead[s] the nations.' The adverb 'justly' translates a Hebrew word that has the sense of evenness, a level place, and the same word appears in Psalm 9:8, where God governs the peoples 'with equity,' and in Psalm 98:9. A level field is one where no one is favoured, and the psalm pictures a world in which the nations, who have so often known oppression under human rulers, meet a judge who is even-handed. The verb 'lead' is the word for guiding along a path, as a shepherd guides, and it gives a pastoral colour to the picture. The nations are not simply ruled; they are led.

The refrain of verses 3 and 5 uses a verb 'praise' that is also the root of 'thanks' and 'confession.' To praise God in Hebrew is to acknowledge publicly what He has done. And the last verse uses a different word from the one many might expect. Where other psalms call the nations to 'praise,' verse 7 says they 'shall fear Him,' yare. The word means awe and reverence, the stance of a creature before a holy God, and in the Old Testament it is the ordinary word for the worship of the true God, as in Psalm 22:23 and Psalm 33:8. One more small point: the word for 'harvest' in verse 6 means produce or increase and is used for the yield of the earth, the same gift that Leviticus 26:4 and Deuteronomy 11:14 say follows obedience. The psalm sees that gift not as a contract but as a witness.

typology.type: The Aaronic blessing turned outward, verses 1 and 2
typology.fulfillment: The priests blessed Israel with the face of God shining on them, Numbers 6:24-26. The psalm sings that blessing and then points it at the world. In Christ the correspondence becomes exact: God's glory shines 'in the face of Christ,' 2 Corinthians 4:6, and the blessing promised to Abraham comes to the Gentiles in Him, Galatians 3:14. The escalation is that the blessing is no longer kept within a nation but is given to all who believe. The type falls short in that the priests could only speak a blessing, while Christ is Himself the blessing, and in Him the face of God is not veiled, John 14:9.

typology.type: The nations glad and singing, verses 3 to 5
typology.fulfillment: The refrain pictures peoples who praise God together, which Israel could not yet see. Paul says this has begun, quoting psalms on the Gentiles' praise in Romans 15:9-11, and Revelation 7:9-10 shows the multitude fulfilling it, crying out 'Salvation belongs to our God.' The escalation is from a hope to a great assembly made of every nation. The type falls short because the psalm has praise from peoples, and does not say how they would be brought in, while the New Testament says it is through the cross, Ephesians 2:13-18.

typology.type: The harvest and the blessing, verses 6 and 7
typology.fulfillment: The earth yields its produce as a sign of God's favour. In the gospel the harvest imagery broadens. Jesus speaks of a harvest of people, Matthew 9:37-38 and John 4:35-38, and says that a grain of wheat that dies bears much fruit, John 12:24, which He applies to His own death and the people who will follow. The escalation is that the crop is now a people from all nations, gathered in by His death and the Spirit's work. The type falls short in that an Israelite harvest could fail, but the harvest of the gospel will be completed, Revelation 14:14-16.

study.christ:
The plain force of Psalm 67 is that the blessing given to one people exists for the sake of all peoples, and that idea has a face in Christ. He is the promised seed of Abraham in whom all nations are blessed, Galatians 3:16 and 3:8, and the one in whom the face of God has become visible, 2 Corinthians 4:6. The Aaronic blessing asked that God's face shine on His people. In Jesus the light shines in a human face, John 1:14, and Simeon's words hold both sides of the psalm together: He is 'a light for revelation to the Gentiles and the glory of Your people Israel,' Luke 2:32.

The psalm's prayer that God's 'salvation' be known among all nations is answered in His own name, since yeshuah is the noun from which 'Jesus' comes, and the angel tells Joseph to give that name to the child because He will save His people from their sins, Matthew 1:21. Peter says that there is salvation in no one else and that no other name has been given under heaven by which we must be saved, Acts 4:12. What the psalm desired in the hope of a future day, the New Testament announces as present news.

Christ also gives the psalm its method. Verse 4's picture of a God who 'judge[s] the peoples justly and lead[s] the nations' is realised in the risen Lord who is given authority over all nations and sends His church to disciple them, Matthew 28:18-20. The Spirit who has been poured out is how the gospel reaches 'the ends of the earth,' Acts 1:8, which is the very phrase of verse 7. And the closing promise, that the ends of the earth 'shall fear Him,' leads to the great scene where every tongue confesses Jesus as Lord, Philippians 2:10-11.

It is worth being careful not to over-read. The psalm does not mention a Messiah, and it does not need to. Its link with Christ is one of purpose and promise: it asks for a world-wide blessing, and He is how that blessing comes. Paul's use of the psalms of the nations in Romans 15 shows the apostolic way to read them, not as secret riddles about Jesus, but as the hope of Israel which He fulfils. And there is an important note of humility in the psalm's posture. It prays 'may God be gracious,' and all of Christ's gifts are gifts of grace, Ephesians 2:8.
study.god:
Psalm 67 shows God as the giver whose generosity has a purpose. The blessing in verses 1, 6 and 7 is not a reward for keeping a contract; it is grace, and the psalm uses the word 'gracious' without qualification. The purpose is that the world know Him. This is a God who is not content to be known by one nation, who does not guard His goodness as a private possession, and who makes His own people the means by which others come to Him. That changes how His blessing should be received: as a trust and a witness.

The psalm also shows a God who is the judge and guide of every nation. The nations are invited to be glad because He 'judge[s] the peoples justly,' verse 4. The same fact that makes oppressors tremble is good news for the oppressed. A God who is just and leads is neither arbitrary nor weak. He cannot be bribed, flattered or dodged, and therefore every nation can trust Him. Elsewhere Scripture puts this alongside His mercy, as in Psalm 98:9 and Psalm 96:10-13, where the creation rejoices because He comes to judge.

The psalm presents God as the source of the harvest. The earth yields, but 'God, our God, blesses us.' The fields belong to Him. In a culture where the gods of the land were credited with the rains and the crops, this was a bold claim, and it was also a pastoral one. The farmer who waits for rain and the seed that dies in the ground are in the hands of a person who can be trusted. Jesus draws on the same conviction when He says the Father sends rain on the just and the unjust, Matthew 5:45, and Paul when he tells the Athenians that God gives rain and fruitful seasons, Acts 14:17.

Finally, the psalm shows something about the heart of God. He is not like a king who fears the nations' rivalry. He wants their praise to be glad and their singing to be for joy. Its refrain asks for all peoples, and the word 'all' appears in the psalm twice in the refrain and once more in 'all the ends of the earth.' The God of Israel is not a tribal deity. For worship, this means that a church that prays this psalm should be praying for the nations as well as for itself, and that its own joys and harvests are to be offered as evidence that God is good, not as private possession.

crossReferences.note: The priestly blessing that supplies the psalm's first line. It asks that the LORD bless, keep, shine and be gracious, and Psalm 67:1 takes those words and adds 'that Your ways may be known on earth.' The psalm reads the ancient blessing as a missionary prayer.

God promises to bless Abraham so that he will be a blessing and so that all the families of the earth will be blessed through him. It supplies the ground for Psalm 67:1-2, where blessing on one people is asked so that the whole earth may know God's ways.

The promise is repeated after the offering of Isaac: 'in your offspring all the nations of the earth will be blessed.' It shows that the nations' blessing is part of God's covenant from the start, and it lies behind the psalm's prayer for all the peoples.

Solomon's prayer asks God to hear the foreigner who prays toward the temple, so that all the peoples of the earth will know and fear Him. It is nearly the same hope as Psalm 67:7 in the setting of the temple dedication.

The shortest psalm calls all nations to praise the LORD for His loving devotion and faithfulness. It gives the answer to which Psalm 67:3 and 5 are the prayer, and it shows how the Psalter ties the nations' praise to God's steadfast love.

The LORD comes to judge the earth, the world with righteousness and the peoples with equity. It is close to Psalm 67:4 and shows that the nations' joy in God's judging is a settled theme, in which His even-handed rule is good news.

The servant is given as a light for the nations, so that God's salvation may reach to the ends of the earth. The phrase 'ends of the earth' appears in Psalm 67:7, and Paul and Barnabas quote this verse in Acts 13:47 to explain the turn to the Gentiles.

Paul strings together Old Testament calls for the Gentiles to praise God, including 'Praise the Lord, all you Gentiles.' He reads those calls, of which Psalm 67:3 is a close cousin, as the aim of Christ's ministry, so that Gentiles glorify God for His mercy.

Scripture foresaw that God would justify the Gentiles by faith and preached the gospel to Abraham in advance, saying 'All nations will be blessed through you.' It explains why the psalm's prayer for the nations is rooted in the original promise and was always about the gospel.

God, who said 'Let light shine out of darkness,' has made His light shine in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God 'in the face of Christ.' It gives the New Testament fulfilment of the psalm's prayer that God's face would shine.

A great multitude from every nation, tribe, people and language stands before the throne and cries out that salvation belongs to God. It is the picture that Psalm 67:3-5 prays for, where all the peoples praise, glad and singing.

study.oneStory:
Psalm 67 answers a question that hangs over the Bible from Genesis 11 onward. After Babel the nations are scattered, and the narrative narrows to one family. Why? Genesis 12:2-3 gives the reply: God chose Abraham in order to bless every family of the earth through him. Psalm 67 picks up that reply and puts it in the mouth of the congregation. It is an acknowledgement that Israel's election was for a purpose beyond itself, and a prayer that the purpose be carried out.

The psalm also meets the problem of the harvest. In the garden God gave food freely, Genesis 1:29 and 2:16, and after the fall the ground was cursed, Genesis 3:17-19. Each good harvest is a small reversal of that curse, a reminder that God still feeds His creatures. Psalm 67:6 sees in each harvest a gift from God's own hand, and that gift is designed to lead beyond itself, to the nations' knowledge of the Giver. The fruit of the field is a first instalment of the fruit of the Spirit.

What it sets up is the mission of the church. The risen Christ says that all authority is His and sends His followers to disciple all nations, Matthew 28:18-20. Acts shows the pattern in action: Peter's vision at Joppa, Acts 10, the first Gentile believers at Antioch, Acts 11:19-26, and the council at Jerusalem where James sees the prophets' vision of a gathering of nations, Acts 15:13-18. The psalm's word 'ends of the earth' is used in Acts 1:8 as the horizon of the church's witness. Paul's ministry in Romans 15 is an explicit fulfilment, and his plan to take the gospel to Spain shows the psalm's vision still moving outward.

The story ends with the nations gathered. Revelation 5:9 says the Lamb ransomed people for God from every tribe and language and people and nation, and Revelation 7:9-10 shows them before the throne. Revelation 21:24-26 has the nations bringing their glory into the city, and Revelation 22:2 says the leaves of the tree of life are for the healing of the nations. The harvest that Psalm 67 sings of is the beginning of a much larger ingathering, and the last line, 'that all the ends of the earth shall fear Him,' is finally true in the new creation, where the nations are no longer strangers to God but His people.

quiz.q: What earlier biblical blessing does this psalm's opening verse echo?

options.text: The Aaronic priestly blessing of Numbers 6:24-26.
options.note: The prayer for God's grace and shining face directly echoes this earlier blessing, now redirected toward the nations.

options.text: The blessing given to Jacob before his death.
options.note: The psalm's specific language of grace and God's shining face echoes the priestly blessing of Numbers 6, not Jacob's deathbed blessing.

options.text: The blessing pronounced at Solomon's coronation.
options.note: No coronation blessing is echoed here; the language is from the priestly blessing of Numbers 6.

options.text: The blessing given to Noah after the flood.
options.note: The psalm's language specifically matches the Aaronic priestly blessing, not the blessing given to Noah.

quiz.q: According to verse 2, why does the psalmist want God to bless and be gracious to His people?

options.text: So that God's way and salvation would become known among all nations.
options.note: The blessing on Israel is explicitly requested for the sake of the nations knowing God.

options.text: So that Israel alone would prosper, with no concern for other nations.
options.note: The verse explicitly states the purpose extends to all nations knowing God's salvation.

options.text: So that Israel could defeat its enemies in battle.
options.note: The stated purpose is that God's way be known among the nations, not military victory.

options.text: So that the priests alone would have access to God's presence.
options.note: The purpose given extends to all nations, not merely priestly access.

quiz.q: What quality of God's rule over the nations does verse 4 highlight?

options.text: He judges the peoples justly and leads the nations of the earth.
options.note: This grounds the nations' invited joy in God's just and guiding rule over them.

options.text: He is indifferent to how the nations are governed.
options.note: The verse specifically credits God with just judgment and active leading of the nations.

options.text: He rules only over Israel, leaving other nations ungoverned.
options.note: The verse explicitly extends God's just judgment and guidance to the nations broadly.

options.text: He allows the nations to govern themselves entirely apart from Him.
options.note: The verse presents God as actively judging and leading the nations, not leaving them entirely to themselves.

quiz.q: What tangible sign of blessing does the psalm mention in verse 6?

options.text: The earth has yielded its harvest.
options.note: This concrete agricultural blessing grounds the psalm's larger missionary hope in a specific, tangible provision.

options.text: A military victory over a foreign army.
options.note: The tangible sign named is a harvest, not a military victory.

options.text: The construction of a new temple.
options.note: No temple construction is mentioned; the sign given is agricultural harvest.

options.text: The appointment of a new king.
options.note: The specific blessing named is the earth's harvest, not a political appointment.

quiz.q: How does the New Testament fulfill this psalm's closing hope that 'all the ends of the earth' would fear God?

options.text: In the vision of a great multitude from every nation, tribe, and language gathered to praise God and the Lamb.
options.note: Revelation 7:9-10 pictures exactly this psalm's hope realized in full.

options.text: In the complete destruction of every nation except Israel.
options.note: The fulfillment envisioned is worship gathered from every nation, not the destruction of all but Israel.

options.text: In a single future nation replacing all others entirely.
options.note: The fulfillment described is a multitude drawn from every existing nation, tribe, and language, not a single replacement nation.

options.text: In the abolition of all worship everywhere.
options.note: The fulfillment is the flourishing, not the abolition, of worship, now directed to God and the Lamb from every nation.

questions: The psalm prays for God's blessing on His people specifically so that His way would be known among the nations. What blessing has God given you that could become a means of making Him known to someone else?

The psalm's refrain calls 'all the peoples' to praise God, not Israel alone. Who in your life, from a different background or culture than your own, could you specifically pray would come to know and praise God?
Verse 4 grounds the nations' joy in God's just judgment and guidance over them. How does trusting that God actively governs even the nations, not just individuals, shape how you view world events?

The psalm connects a tangible harvest, verse 6, to its larger missionary hope. What ordinary, practical blessing in your own life this season could you specifically dedicate to God's larger purposes rather than keeping only for yourself?

This psalm's hope that all the earth would fear God is fulfilled in the Great Commission and in the vision of every nation gathered in worship. What is one concrete step you could take this week toward participating in that mission, whether through prayer, giving, or going?

translationNotes.note: Cause His face to shine upon us echoes the Aaronic priestly blessing of Numbers 6:24-26 nearly word for word, here redirected from a purely domestic blessing toward a missionary purpose.
Judge the peoples justly can also carry the sense of governing or guiding with equity, describing God's active, righteous rule over every nation, not only Israel.
Fear renders yare, reverent awe rather than mere terror, describing the right response of worship the psalm hopes will extend to every nation on earth.
